Getting text out of files

Source: vignettes/ingest.Rmd
ingest.Rmd

Before a model can read a document, harnessr has to get the text out of the file. That step, ingestion, is easy to overlook and hard to undo. Text lost here, or damaged by too much clean-up, stays lost or damaged: no later step restores it. This guide covers what harnessr can read, what it keeps and removes, and how to check a folder before you spend anything on it.

Ingestion makes no model calls, so it rests on only two pieces of the core. The token counts in doc$stats and in gr_inventory() come from the counter that “Counting tokens” in vignette("models") describes. The cost floor that gr_inventory() reports uses the prices you set, as “Prices” in vignette("models") shows. vignette("core") covers the model calls that later steps make, and vignette("harnessr") introduces the package.

library(harnessr)
old <- hr_options(verbose = FALSE)

What ingestion produces

gr_ingest() reads a file and returns a document: the text split into blocks, which are the paragraphs, headings and list items as the file has them. harnessr includes a short example, an annual report written in Markdown:

doc <- gr_ingest(gr_example())
doc
#> <gr_document> /home/runner/work/_temp/Library/harnessr/extdata/annual_report.md
#>   17 blocks, ~574 tokens, 1846 chars (12 removed by cleaning)
#>   cleaners: page_numbers, hyphenation, control_chars, ligatures, collapse_whitespace
#>   first block: # Northwind Instruments — Annual Report 2024

Each block records where it came from: the page, for formats that have pages, and the section heading it sits under:

doc$blocks[1:6, c("block_id", "page", "section", "kind")]
#>   block_id page                                    section    kind
#> 1        1   NA Northwind Instruments — Annual Report 2024 heading
#> 2        2   NA                                    Summary heading
#> 3        3   NA                                    Summary    body
#> 4        4   NA                                    Summary    body
#> 5        5   NA                                 Operations heading
#> 6        6   NA                                 Operations    body

This record, the provenance, lets an answer point back to its source: ans$evidence reports the page and section of every chunk an answer rests on. page is NA here because Markdown has no pages; a PDF fills it in.

doc$text is all the blocks joined, and doc$stats summarises the document:

unlist(doc$stats[c("blocks", "chars", "tokens", "chars_removed")])
#>        blocks         chars        tokens chars_removed 
#>            17          1846           574            12

answer_document() calls gr_ingest() for you, so you rarely need it yourself. Call it directly to see what the model will get.

What harnessr can read

harnessr reads each file type with an extractor, chosen by the file’s extension. available says whether the packages it needs are installed:

gr_extractors()[, c("name", "extensions", "available")]
#>        name                          extensions available
#> txt     txt            txt, text, log, csv, tsv      TRUE
#> md       md              md, markdown, rmd, qmd      TRUE
#> html   html                    html, htm, xhtml      TRUE
#> pdf     pdf                                 pdf      TRUE
#> docx   docx                          docx, dotx      TRUE
#> image image png, jpg, jpeg, tif, tiff, bmp, gif      TRUE
extractor what it keeps needs
txt paragraphs, split at blank lines nothing
md paragraphs, plus headings as sections and code blocks and tables marked as such nothing
html the text of the page in reading order, with <h1> to <h6> as sections and each table row as one block, its cells joined by a vertical bar; scripts, styles, navigation bars and footers are dropped xml2
docx paragraphs, with headings as sections in any interface language; each table row as one block, its cells joined by a vertical bar; footnotes and endnotes after the paragraph that cites them; images inside the file are read by OCR when tesseract is installed xml2
pdf the text of each page in reading order, with its page number and headings as sections; pages with no text are read by OCR pdftools (and tesseract and magick for OCR)
image the text in a picture, by OCR tesseract

harnessr does not read a file whose extension no extractor claims, such as an old .doc or a spreadsheet. gr_inventory(), below, finds those files before a run, not during one.

You can also pass text directly. gr_ingest() reads a string that is not the path of an existing file as the document itself:

memo <- gr_ingest("Revenue rose to 45.2 million dollars.\n\nHeadcount grew to 1,204.")
memo$blocks[, c("block_id", "text")]
#>   block_id                                  text
#> 1        1 Revenue rose to 45.2 million dollars.
#> 2        2              Headcount grew to 1,204.

A string that ends in an extension some extractor claims, but names no file, is an error:

gr_ingest("anual-report.pdf")
#> Error in `gr_ingest()`:
#> ! File not found: 'anual-report.pdf'. If you meant to pass document text rather than a path, it must not end in something that looks like a file extension.

gr_ingest() reads any other string as text, including a path whose extension is mistyped or is one no extractor claims. If the string looks like a path (it has a / and an extension), you also get a warning, because the answer that follows would be about a file name:

typo <- gr_ingest("reports/2024/annual-report.pfd")
#> Warning in gr_ingest("reports/2024/annual-report.pfd"):
#> 'reports/2024/annual-report.pfd' is not an existing file, and '.pfd' is not an
#> extension harnessr reads, so the string itself is being read as the document.
#> If it is a path, check it; harnessr reads .bmp, .csv, .docx, .dotx, .gif, .htm,
#> .html, .jpeg, .jpg, .log, .markdown, .md, .pdf, .png, .qmd, .rmd, .text, .tif,
#> .tiff, .tsv, .txt, .xhtml.
typo$text
#> [1] "reports/2024/annual-report.pfd"
typo$source
#> [1] "<inline text>"

source tells the two apart. It holds the path when gr_ingest() read a file, and <inline text> when it read the string itself.

gr_ingest() downloads a web address and reads it with the extractor for what the server sent back. It looks, in order, at:

  1. a specific type the server declares;
  2. the extension in the address;
  3. the first bytes of the file, which identify a PDF, a Word file or an HTML page however they were labelled.

gr_ingest() refuses a download no extractor reads; it does not fall back to reading it as text. source holds the address, and a failed download is an error that says why:

doc <- gr_ingest("https://example.org/reports/annual-report-2024.pdf")
doc$source
#> [1] "https://example.org/reports/annual-report-2024.pdf"

Within a session, harnessr downloads an address once and serves later reads of it from the cache, as it does for a file.

Sections and headings

In Markdown, HTML, Word and PDF files, each block records the heading it falls under (the next section says how harnessr finds a PDF’s headings). The example report has these sections:

unique(doc$blocks$section)
#> [1] "Northwind Instruments — Annual Report 2024"
#> [2] "Summary"                                   
#> [3] "Operations"                                
#> [4] "Risk factors"                              
#> [5] "Outlook"                                   
#> [6] "References"

Later steps use them. The structural way of cutting a document into chunks never lets a chunk straddle two sections (vignette("segment")), and the preview reading strategy plans its reading section by section. A plain text file has no headings, so its blocks have no section.

PDFs

harnessr reads a PDF page by page, and every block carries its page number, so you can trace a quotation to “page 12” rather than to “somewhere in the file”.

pdf_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".pdf")
grDevices::pdf(pdf_file, width = 8.5, height = 11)
for (page in list(c("Summary", "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars in fiscal 2024."),
                  c("Outlook", "The board expects revenue of 50 million dollars in 2025."))) {
  graphics::plot.new()
  graphics::text(0, c(0.95, 0.9), page, adj = 0)
}
invisible(grDevices::dev.off())

report <- gr_ingest(pdf_file)
report$blocks[, c("page", "section", "kind", "text")]
#>   page section    kind                                                     text
#> 1    1 Summary heading                                                  Summary
#> 2    1 Summary    body         Revenue was 45.2 million dollars in fiscal 2024.
#> 3    2 Summary    body                                                  Outlook
#> 4    2 Summary    body The board expects revenue of 50 million dollars in 2025.

A PDF’s text comes out in the order of the page layout, which is not always the order a person reads in. harnessr puts it back in reading order:

  • A page set in two columns is read one column after the other. Without this, each line would join the start of a line from each column.
  • Running heads and feet (short lines repeated at the top or bottom of many pages, such as a journal name or “Page 3 of 12”) are removed.
  • harnessr finds headings, so blocks carry sections as they do for Markdown and Word. It takes them from the PDF’s bookmarks when the PDF has them. Otherwise a line that is only a standard section name (“Introduction”, “2. Methods”, “Results”) counts. That is how harnessr found “Summary” above; “Outlook” is not a standard name, so it stayed text.

gr_ingest_spec(layout = "raw") turns all three off and keeps each page as it is laid out. Footnotes, tables and pages in three or more columns can still come out in an order that reads oddly, so check a few pages of report$text before relying on a new kind of PDF.

Scanned pages and OCR

A scanned PDF is a picture of text, with no text inside it to extract. To read it, harnessr needs optical character recognition (OCR), which turns the picture back into text. OCR is slow (seconds per page) and never perfect, so by default harnessr runs it only on pages that need it:

# The default: OCR any page with fewer than 40 characters of text.
gr_ingest("scan.pdf", gr_ingest_spec(ocr = "auto"))

# A page with a little text but mostly scanned content: raise the threshold.
gr_ingest("scan.pdf", gr_ingest_spec(ocr = "auto", ocr_min_chars = 200))

# Everything, or nothing.
gr_ingest("scan.pdf", gr_ingest_spec(ocr = "always"))
gr_ingest("born-digital.pdf", gr_ingest_spec(ocr = "never"))

# Another language, at a higher resolution.
gr_ingest("scan.pdf", gr_ingest_spec(ocr_lang = "deu", ocr_dpi = 400))

OCR on PDFs needs both tesseract and magick. Without them a scanned page comes back nearly empty and harnessr warns (gr_ocr_unavailable). The document lists those pages in doc$stats$unread_pages, and harnessr marks an answer drawn from it as partial. The same holds with ocr = "never": harnessr lists a page with no text, or only a stamp or a running head, as unread. A document with too little text left is refused outright, as “When too little text is left” below shows. The "scanned" recipe is set up for this kind of document.

Cleaning

Extracted text is rarely clean. PDFs break words across lines with hyphens, repeat the page number on every page, and use typographic ligatures (“ﬁ” for “fi”). harnessr tidies this with cleaners. Each does one job, and you can turn each on or off:

gr_cleaners()[, c("name", "stage", "default_on")]
#>                   name stage default_on
#> 1             captions early      FALSE
#> 2               emails early      FALSE
#> 3      headers_footers early      FALSE
#> 4          hyphenation early       TRUE
#> 5         page_numbers early       TRUE
#> 6           references early      FALSE
#> 7                 urls early      FALSE
#> 8           ascii_only  late      FALSE
#> 9  collapse_whitespace  late       TRUE
#> 10       control_chars  late       TRUE
#> 11           ligatures  late       TRUE
#> 12           lowercase  late      FALSE
#> 13      remove_numbers  late      FALSE
#> 14  remove_punctuation  late      FALSE

The five marked default_on run unless you turn them off. The others are off by default. The ones below are off for these reasons:

  • remove_numbers replaces every digit with a space, which makes any question about a figure, date or percentage unanswerable.
  • captions removes lines that look like figure and table captions, which destroys documents made mostly of tables.
  • urls and emails remove links and addresses, which are sometimes the answer.
  • references cuts everything from a line reading just “References”, “Bibliography” or “Works cited” to the end of the document. It cuts only when that line starts at or after 40% of the text, so a table of contents near the start does not cut the document. The line may be numbered (“7. References”) or a Markdown heading (“## References”); a line inside a fenced code block is not a heading. cleaner_opts = list(references_after = ) moves that share, a number from 0 to 1. If your question is about the sources, the cut loses the reference list you need.

No reader can recover what a cleaner removes, so know what each choice costs before you make it.

Presets

Instead of naming cleaners one by one, use a preset:

preset what it runs
"none" nothing
"minimal" control characters and whitespace only
"standard" the default: page numbers, broken hyphens, control characters, ligatures, whitespace
"academic" standard, plus captions and references
"scan" standard, plus repeated page headers and footers
"legacy" what the first version of this package did, number stripping included; for comparison only

Each preset leaves this many characters of the example report:

presets <- c("none", "minimal", "standard", "academic", "scan", "legacy")
vapply(presets, function(p) gr_ingest(gr_example(), gr_ingest_spec(clean = p))$stats$chars,
       integer(1))
#>     none  minimal standard academic     scan   legacy 
#>     1858     1858     1846     1655     1846     1558

Or name the cleaners yourself:

tidy <- gr_ingest(gr_example(),
                  gr_ingest_spec(clean = c("page_numbers", "hyphenation", "collapse_whitespace")))
tidy$stats$chars
#> [1] 1846

Seeing what cleaning removed

Every document records what each cleaner took out, in characters:

vapply(doc$stats$clean_log, function(step) step$chars_removed, integer(1))
#>        page_numbers         hyphenation       control_chars           ligatures 
#>                  12                   0                   0                   0 
#> collapse_whitespace 
#>                   0

A negative number means a cleaner added characters, for example by expanding “ﬁ” to “fi”. If a cleaner removed far more than you expected, turn it off and compare.

gr_clean() runs cleaners on any text, so you can try a configuration on a few of your own lines first. Cleaners always run in two stages, early before late, whatever order you list them in. Without the stages, number removal could strip the “1” from “Page 1” before the page-number cleaner recognised the line:

cleaned <- gr_clean(c("Page 1", "Revenue rose to 45.2 million in 2024."),
                    steps = c("remove_numbers", "page_numbers"))
as.character(cleaned)
#> [1] ""                                  "Revenue rose to  .  million in  ."

The second line shows why remove_numbers is off by default.

When too little text is left

harnessr refuses a document with almost no text after cleaning (a scan read without OCR, an empty file, a PDF of images) instead of sending it to the model. A model shown nothing would answer “not in the document” for a document that may well contain the answer:

gr_ingest("Tiny.")
#> Error in `gr_ingest()`:
#> ! Only 5 characters survived ingestion of '<inline text>' (minimum 20). The file may be empty, image-only with OCR disabled, or your cleaning steps may be too aggressive: 0 characters were removed by cleaners: page_numbers(-0) hyphenation(-0) control_chars(-0) ligatures(-0) collapse_whitespace(-0).

min_chars in gr_ingest_spec() sets the limit, 20 characters by default.

Reading the same file twice

harnessr caches each ingestion in memory for the R session. A second question about the same file, or a different way of cutting it into chunks, reuses the extracted text instead of reading the file again. The cache key holds the file’s size and modification time and every ingestion setting, so harnessr reads the file again when any of them changes. The cache holds about 256 MB of documents; past that, harnessr drops the ones used least recently and reads them again when next asked for. Turn the cache off with hr_options(cache_documents = FALSE).

Before reading a whole folder

In a folder of documents, problems that a single file makes obvious are easy to miss: a few old .doc files nobody can read, scanned PDFs without text, an empty file, or a subfolder you forgot about. gr_inventory() finds all of these in seconds, without calling a model and without an API key. Its cost floor needs your model’s price, which harnessr does not ship (“Prices” in vignette("models")), so the example sets one first:

# Illustrative figures, in USD per million tokens: use your provider's current
# prices.
hr_register_model(hr_options("model"), input_usd = 2, output_usd = 12)

inbox <- file.path(tempdir(), "inbox")
dir.create(inbox, showWarnings = FALSE)
invisible(file.copy(gr_example(), file.path(inbox, "annual_report.md"),
                    overwrite = TRUE))
writeLines("Headcount grew to 1,204 employees across nine sites.",
           file.path(inbox, "notes.txt"))
writeLines("(a Word 97 document)", file.path(inbox, "minutes.doc"))
invisible(file.create(file.path(inbox, "empty.txt")))

inv <- gr_inventory(inbox)
inv
#> <gr_inventory> /tmp/RtmpH7Q2zW/inbox
#>   4 file(s), 1.9 KB; 2 readable
#>   2 ready, 1 no_extractor, 1 empty
#>   tokens: 549   cost floor: $0.01 (gpt-5.6-terra, one call per document), prices as of 2026-11
#>   ! 1 file(s) would be skipped: .doc (1). gr_register_extractor() adds a format.

It lists every file, including the ones harnessr will not read, so you learn before the run that a file will be skipped:

inv$files[, c("file", "extractor", "status", "tokens")]
#>               file extractor       status tokens
#> 1 annual_report.md        md        ready    531
#> 2        empty.txt       txt        empty     NA
#> 3      minutes.doc      <NA> no_extractor     NA
#> 4        notes.txt       txt        ready     18

The statuses:

status meaning
ready an extractor can read it, and there is text
needs_ocr a PDF whose pages have no text; it needs OCR
needs_package an extractor can read it, but its package is not installed
no_extractor no extractor reads this kind of file
empty nothing to read
unreadable it could not be opened; note says why

It shows three things you would not otherwise see in a corpus run:

what it shows why it matters
files no extractor claims they were dropped without appearing anywhere, so a folder of .doc files read as an empty corpus
PDFs with no text layer they extract to nothing, then answer NOT_IN_DOCUMENT, which looks the same as a document that does not say
files in subfolders they are listed with their folder, so a subfolder you forgot is visible; recursive = FALSE scans one level only

folder is a column, so split(inv$files, inv$files$folder) gives you the piles. gr_inventory() does not choose a recipe for you. A router that quietly read one document with retrieve and another with stuff would hand you a plausible answer built on part of a file, with nothing to say so. It would also make gr_compare() meaningless, because the corpus would no longer have one configuration. Group the rows yourself and pass each group the recipe you picked. vignette("review") covers reading a whole folder.

inv$totals adds up the tokens and prices one request per readable file with your model: the file’s tokens in, and an assumed 500-token answer out. hr_estimate_cost() gives the figure and its priced, as_of and certain columns (“What a cost estimate says: hr_estimate_cost()” in vignette("models")). Treat cost_floor_usd as a rough guide, not a bound. Reading strategies that make several requests per document cost more, and short answers cost less. The total leaves out files whose size is unknown until OCR reads them; tokens_unknown counts those.

unlist(inv$totals[c("readable", "tokens", "cost_floor_usd")])
#>       readable         tokens cost_floor_usd 
#>       2.000000     549.000000       0.013098

Choosing the settings

Two groups of ingest settings change what the model gets: cleaning and OCR. Each walkthrough below covers:

  • what the setting controls and what it trades off;
  • the signs in your results that point to changing it;
  • where its default came from;
  • how to test a change.

vignette("settings") lists every ingest setting with its default.

The tests use hr_sweep(), which builds one arm per value of a setting, and hr_benchmark(), which runs every arm on a reference of questions. Here they run on one question and a stand-in model that always gives the right answer. That shows how to build and read a sweep, but cannot show which value is better. vignette("compare") runs sweeps on a reference with dev and test splits and reads them with intervals.

qa <- gr_qa_reference(questions = c(revenue = "What was revenue in 2024?"),
                      documents = gr_example(), answers = list("45.2 million"),
                      split = "dev")
says <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")

Cleaning presets and references_after

What it controls. clean chooses the cleaners that run on the extracted text, by preset or by name (see “Presets” above), and cleaner_opts = list(references_after = ) sets where the references cleaner may cut. Cleaning trades noise against loss. Page numbers, running heads and captions cost tokens and can mislead retrieval, but text an overeager cleaner removes is gone for good, and no later setting brings it back.

Signs it needs changing. An answer of NOT_IN_DOCUMENT for a fact you can see in the file, or a quotation that fails verification, can mean a cleaner removed the text. Look in doc$stats$clean_log for a cleaner that removed far more than the others. If answers quote page headers or figure captions as if they were findings, move the other way, to "academic" or "scan". Under "academic", if an answer about a paper’s sources says they are not in the document, the reference list was cut. A document whose table of contents has a “References” line after the first 40% of its text is cut at that line; raise references_after for such documents.

Where the defaults came from. "standard" is the preset meant for born-digital text and has not been compared with the others. references_after is 0.4, the value set when the cleaner was written. Both are untested in gr_settings_table("ingest").

How to test it. Sweep the presets and look at what was sent:

arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("fast"), list(clean = c("standard", "academic", "scan", "none")))
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = says, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.clean, bench, mean)
#>   param.clean tokens_in
#> 1    academic       549
#> 2        none       619
#> 3        scan       611
#> 4    standard       611
hr_sweep_check(bench)
#>               arm             same_as runs requests                settings
#> 1 fast:clean=scan fast:clean=standard    5        5 clean: standard vs scan

On the example report, "academic" sends 62 fewer prompt tokens than "standard", because it drops the caption lines and the reference list after the ## References heading. "none" sends 8 more. hr_sweep_check() finds that "scan" sent exactly the requests "standard" sent. The example has no running heads, so on it that comparison would measure only run-to-run spread. The same check tells you whether a references_after sweep reaches your documents at all:

arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("fast", list(clean = "academic")),
                 data.frame(cleaner_opts = I(list(list(references_after = 0.4),
                                                  list(references_after = 0.8)))))
hr_sweep_check(hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = says, split = "dev",
                            scorer = gr_scorer_answer()))
#>                                              arm
#> 1 fast:cleaner_opts=list(references_after = 0.8)
#>                                          same_as runs requests
#> 1 fast:cleaner_opts=list(references_after = 0.4)    5        5
#>                                                                     settings
#> 1 cleaner_opts: list(references_after = 0.4) vs list(references_after = 0.8)

Both values sent the same requests. The example report’s ## References heading starts 94% of the way through its text, after both 40% and 80%, so both values cut the text at the same line. A references_after sweep changes what is sent only for a document whose heading falls between the two values. Run it on your own documents, with questions whose answers sit near the end.

OCR settings

What it controls. ocr decides which pages harnessr reads as pictures:

  • "auto" reads a page by OCR only when it has fewer than ocr_min_chars characters of text (40);
  • "always" reads every page that way;
  • "never" reads none.

ocr_trigger says which text those characters are counted on: "raw_text" counts the page’s whole text layer, and "after_running_lines" counts what is left once the layout pass has dropped running heads, feet and stamps. ocr_dpi is the resolution the page is rendered at, and ocr_lang the Tesseract language. OCR costs seconds per page and adds recognition errors; skipping it on a scanned page leaves that page empty.

The blocks of a page read by OCR have kind = "ocr" (its headings keep "heading"). ocr_confidence = TRUE gives them an ocr_confidence column, Tesseract’s mean word confidence for the page, from 0 to 100. It runs a second Tesseract pass over each OCR-ed page, so OCR takes about twice as long. It is off by default.

Signs it needs changing. doc$stats$unread_pages lists pages that came back empty, and harnessr marks an answer from such a document as partial. A scanned page with a printed header or stamp can carry more than 40 characters of text and so skip OCR under "auto". Set ocr_trigger = "after_running_lines" when the stamp repeats on every page, or raise ocr_min_chars when it does not. Under ocr_confidence = TRUE, if the blocks an answer cites have a low ocr_confidence, read that page yourself. If OCR text has misread numbers or letters (a quotation fails verification against a page that plainly says it), try a higher ocr_dpi or the right ocr_lang.

Where the defaults came from. ocr_dpi = 300 follows Tesseract’s documentation on improving output quality (cited). ocr = "auto" runs OCR only where a page has no text layer, and no other choice has been compared. ocr_min_chars = 40 was set when OCR was added and has not been tuned, and ocr_lang = "eng" is English because the package’s own examples are in English. ocr_trigger = "raw_text" is how pages were chosen before the setting existed, and has not been compared with "after_running_lines". ocr_confidence = FALSE keeps OCR to the one Tesseract pass it always ran. All of them except ocr_dpi are untested.

How to test it. OCR needs a scanned file and the tesseract and magick packages, so run this on your own documents, with a reference you build from them with gr_qa_reference() and your own client:

arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("scanned"), list(ocr_min_chars = c(40, 200, 1000)))
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, my_reference, runs = 5, client = my_client, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(correct ~ param.ocr_min_chars, bench, mean)
hr_sweep_check(bench)

A row from hr_sweep_check() means no page crossed the threshold between that arm’s value and an earlier one, so the two arms read the documents the same way.

Sweep ocr_trigger the same way. It decides which pages OCR reads before any request goes out, so doc$stats$unread_pages and the "ocr" blocks of each ingestion show its effect at no cost:

arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("scanned"),
                 list(ocr_trigger = c("raw_text", "after_running_lines")))
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, my_reference, runs = 5, client = my_client, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(correct ~ param.ocr_trigger, bench, mean)

ocr_confidence changes no text and no request, so a sweep of it shows the same answers. You get the column and pay for the second pass; wrap each gr_ingest() in system.time() to see that cost:

arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("scanned"), list(ocr_confidence = c(FALSE, TRUE)))

Adding your own

You can add a format harnessr does not know, or a clean-up step your documents need, and then use it exactly like a built-in one. This cleaner drops lines marked “CONFIDENTIAL”:

gr_register_cleaner("drop_confidential", stage = "early",
  fn = function(x, opts) gsub("(?mi)^\\s*CONFIDENTIAL.*$", "", x, perl = TRUE),
  description = "Remove lines marked CONFIDENTIAL")

gr_ingest("CONFIDENTIAL - internal only\n\nRevenue rose to 45.2 million dollars.",
          gr_ingest_spec(clean = c("drop_confidential", "collapse_whitespace")))$text
#> [1] "Revenue rose to 45.2 million dollars."

?gr_register_extractor shows how to add a file format, and vignette("extending") covers every kind of addition.

Next

With the text out, you next decide how to cut it into chunks (vignette("segment")) and how the model should read them (vignette("readers")). To read a whole folder once gr_inventory() has checked it, see vignette("review").
